traits.fan_split_depth.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 276): the blade regularly divided nearly to the middle or beyond into single-fold segments; read as free over a half to six tenths of their length. Its segments stiff or flexible and its petiole unarmed or armed with sparse to dense, small or large teeth, so both are left to the species.

traits.segment_filaments.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 276): interfold filaments often present; read as a few threads.

traits.leaf_division.note: Mabberley's Plant-book (4th ed., 2017), under Palmae, subfamily III Coryphoideae: leaves induplicately palmate in all but Phoenix and the Caryoteae (Arenga, Caryota, Wallichia), which are pinnate. A fan palm's blade is one piece cut into segments: simple, parted, palmate.

generator.params.costa.why: The rib the fan's segments rise from, as a share of the frond: a fifth for a strongly costapalmate fan, a tenth for a shortly costapalmate one (the built-in cabbage and California fan palms, 0.18 and 0.12).

generator.params.skirt.why: Dead fronds hang on the stem instead of falling.

generator.params.dead_life.why: How many years a dead frond hangs, set by eye: the book says only that they stay on, and most such palms shed them within a few years (the California fan palm, whose skirt lasts for decades, sets its own).

generator.params.dead_angle.why: A dead frond hangs close against the stem, as the built-in California fan palm's do.

rules.note: Dransfield et al. (Genera Palmarum, 2nd ed., 2008), under the genus: its fan leaves are shortly costapalmate, the rib running only a little into the blade; its dead leaves stay on the stem (marcescent) rather than falling cleanly.

appearance.note: A dead frond drawn as the built-in palms draw theirs: a brown fan for a fan palm, a brown feather frond for a feather palm.
